title: About
lead: {brand} is a training tool for trail runners, mountain hikers and road runners. This page lists the program version, where the calculations come from, the licences of the third-party data and software it uses, and the trademark notice.
version.note: Include both numbers when you report a problem; it makes it easier to look into.
methods.lead: The calculations in this service implement the published literature and methods below; the methods and their names belong to their authors, and this service did not invent them. Numbers marked as estimates are calibrated with your own data; each screen's ? help lists the sources used there.
m.weighted.name: Weighted power, intensity and training load
m.weighted.desc: Weighted power = the fourth root of the mean fourth power of the 30-second rolling average power; Intensity = weighted power ÷ threshold power; training load per hour = Intensity² × 100. The formulas are Coggan's published definitions.
m.load.name: Chronic load, acute load and load balance
m.load.desc: Each day's training load is averaged with exponential weights over time constants of 42 and 7 days, giving the chronic load and the acute load; load balance = the previous day's chronic minus acute. Treating the effect of training as two quantities that fade at different rates comes from the training response model of Banister and colleagues.
m.ramp.name: Weekly increase limit of chronic load
m.ramp.desc: How much the automatic schedule raises the chronic load each week follows Joe Friel's advice on weekly increases; the actual limits are estimates.
m.cp.name: Critical power (CP) and W′
m.cp.desc: The power–duration relation P = CP + W′/t, used to read CP tests, set interval power targets and estimate finish times.
m.pd.name: Power–duration (PD) model
m.pd.desc: A power–duration curve fitted to your best power at each duration over the last 90 days: short durations are dominated by an anaerobic term that falls with time, long durations level off near critical power and decline slowly beyond the sustainable duration. Modelled threshold power, anaerobic capacity and the sustainable duration are read from this fit. Models of the same kind, covering every duration, are found in the published literature.
m.grade.name: Energy cost of gradient (flat equivalent)
m.grade.desc: A polynomial for the energy cost per metre of running uphill and downhill by gradient, used to turn climbing and descending into flat-equivalent effort and to estimate trail pace and finish times.
m.hike.name: Hiking speed
m.hike.desc: Tobler's hiking function (speed changing exponentially with gradient), used for the downhill speed limit and for hiking time estimates.
m.pack.name: Pack weight
m.pack.desc: An equation for the metabolic cost of pack weight, gradient and speed, used for climbing with a pack, the pacing of multi-day Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) trips and steep power hiking conversions.
m.riegel.name: Race distance conversion
m.riegel.desc: A power law (Riegel's formula) that converts a race result to other distances or durations, used to estimate CP and finish times from race results.
m.racecalc.name: Race calculator
m.racecalc.desc: The formulas for environment adjustments (temperature, humidity, altitude), CP and W′ estimates, running effectiveness and finish predictions are ported from Steve Palladino's SuperPower Calculator spreadsheet (a tool shared openly in the running power community); the trail and Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) extensions follow the gradient and pack literature listed on this page.
m.pzones.name: Running power zones
m.pzones.desc: Zones as percentages of CP (Palladino's running power zones), used to describe the intensity of sessions and activities.
m.hrzones.name: Heart rate zones
m.hrzones.desc: By default seven zones as percentages of lactate threshold heart rate (LTHR) (Joe Friel); other models can be chosen.
m.hrmax.name: Maximum heart rate from age
m.hrmax.desc: When there is no maximum heart rate from you, your watch or your runs, it is estimated as 208 − 0.7 × age and marked as an estimate.
m.rpe.name: Training load from perceived effort
m.rpe.desc: Activities without power or heart rate are converted to training load from the Borg CR-10 perceived exertion scale (Foster's session RPE method).
m.aet.name: Aerobic threshold (AeT) test and weekly climbing
m.aet.desc: The heart-rate-drift AeT test and how the weekly climbing target rises and falls follow Uphill Athlete (Scott Johnston, Steve House).
m.reentry.name: Coming back after a break
m.reentry.desc: After a few days to a few weeks without running, the return to your usual training volume in stages follows Jack Daniels' table for returning after a break.
m.heat.name: Heat acclimation
m.heat.desc: The performance penalty in hot conditions and how heat acclimation builds and decays follow the international consensus on training and competing in the heat.
data.lead: The third-party data below appears only on the screens that use it, with its source credited under its licence. It may be inaccurate, out of date or temporarily unavailable; do not rely on it alone to judge a route or the weather.
d.osm.name: OpenStreetMap
d.osm.desc: Map tiles, and the list of mountain huts and campsites in Taiwan (stage-split candidates for multi-day trips). Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0; the hut and campsite list is a derived database of OpenStreetMap, also available under ODbL 1.0.
d.nlsc.name: National Land Surveying and Mapping Center (NLSC), Taiwan
d.nlsc.desc: Taiwan e-Map, orthophoto and road tiles, used under the Open Government Data License, version 1.0 (Taiwan).
d.rudy.name: Rudy Map
d.rudy.desc: Hiking map tiles and the contour overlay, used under Rudy Map's terms; the map data includes OpenStreetMap.
d.baiyue.name: Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) and Little 100 Peaks
d.baiyue.desc: Peak names, elevations and coordinates for summit detection on the achievements page, peak names on routes and the weather location in the race calculator. Points of Taiwan's 100 Peaks (Baiyue) and the Little 100 Peaks: Map Generator by happyman (twmap.happyman.idv.tw); the Baiyue list: Chinese Taipei Mountaineering Association.
d.google.name: Google Maps
d.google.desc: Terrain and road tiles; map data © Google.
d.cwa.name: Central Weather Administration (CWA) open data
d.cwa.desc: Mountain and township weather forecasts (the weather in the race calculator and the schedule), used under the Open Government Data License, version 1.0 (Taiwan); source: Central Weather Administration, Ministry of Transportation and Communications.
d.metno.name: MET Norway (Norwegian Meteorological Institute)
d.metno.desc: Weather forecasts the CWA does not provide (up to 9 days ahead, places outside Taiwan). Data from MET Norway, available under CC BY 4.0.
d.openmeteo.name: Open-Meteo
d.openmeteo.desc: Past climate data (the race-day mean of the same month over 10 years, the weather during each run) and elevation, available under CC BY 4.0. Part of the elevation data comes from the Copernicus GLO-90 DEM: © DLR e.V. 2010–2014 and © Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014–2018, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA.

cairn.what: Cairn is our other service, for planning hiking trips: where each day ends and where you sleep on a timeline, the 3D terrain and the trail surface, your live position shared with the family who stay behind once you set off, and group sign-ups. {brand} covers the training before you go and how long the trip will take, how to pace it and how much to eat, so the two complement each other. Cairn makes a free account the first time you sign in with Google.
cairn.routes: Routes go both ways: paste a Cairn trip's share link in the Race manager and the route and each night's stop become that race's GPX; once it is worked out, you can push the route, the pacing curve and the overnight stops to Cairn (with your accounts linked, on a paid plan). The steps are in the manual's Cairn section.
cairn.link: The same Google account is never linked on its own: you link it in the Cairn tab of Settings, or you are asked the first time something is to be pushed. Once linked, Cairn can read only the items listed — never your activities, heart rate or other health data — and you can unlink at any time.
legal.lead: The documents you agree to when you sign up: the rules for using this service, how we handle your data, and the health-risk and third-party notices.
